hints: Remember the naming order for a dipeptide, the first named amino acid keeps its free $\text{NH}_2$ group on the left and provides its $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ group to form the peptide link.
Look up the R groups in the Data Booklet, glu has $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ and cys has $\text{CH}_2\text{SH}$, and join the two alpha carbons through $\text{CO-NH}$.
walkthrough:
Place the two amino acids in the correct order**
Think of a dipeptide as written left to right from the N terminus to the C terminus. For glu-cys, glutamic acid is on the left so it keeps its $\text{H}_2\text{N-CH}$ end free, and cysteine is on the right so it keeps its $\text{CH-CO}_2\text{H}$ end free. The link forms between them in the middle.

Form the peptide link by condensation**
Join the carboxyl carbon of glu to the nitrogen of cys with loss of water to give $\text{-CO-NH-}$. So the backbone becomes $\text{H}_2\text{N-CH-CO-NH-CH-CO}_2\text{H}$. That central $\text{CONH}$ is the mark for the peptide bond, draw it fully displayed.

Add the correct side chains**
Now attach the R groups to the two alpha carbons. On the left alpha carbon add the glu side chain $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H}$, on the right alpha carbon add the cys side chain $\text{CH}_2\text{SH}$. Check that every carbon has four bonds and you have not lost the terminal $\text{NH}_2$ and $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ groups.

Final answer: $\text{H}_2\text{NCH}(\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H})\text{CONHCH}(\text{CH}_2\text{SH})\text{CO}_2\text{H}$
Correct peptide link $\text{CO-NH}$ with glu residue on left ($\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ side chain) and cys residue on right ($\text{CH}_2\text{SH}$ side chain).

hints: Look at the direction of movement, all spots that move toward the positive (+) electrode must carry an overall negative charge, while a spot that stays at the origin must be essentially neutral.
Compare the structures at the electrophoresis pH, cys can exist as a zwitterion with balanced charges whereas glu and glu-cys both carry extra $\text{CO}_2^-$ groups from the acidic side chain.
For the two negatively charged species, think about what else controls speed besides charge, and compare the $M_r$ of free glu with the larger dipeptide glu-cys.
walkthrough:
Read the electrophoresis pattern**
Picture what the field does. The (+) plate is on the left and the mixture starts on the right. Spots E and F have migrated left toward (+), so they are anions. Spot G has hardly moved from the application point, so it has essentially zero net charge under these conditions.

Assign the neutral spot**
Cysteine at this pH exists largely as the zwitterion, $\text{H}_3\text{N}^+\text{-CH(R)-CO}_2^-$, where the positive ammonium and negative carboxylate cancel. With no overall charge there is no electrical force to pull it, so G must be cys. That explains the smallest movement.

Separate glu from glu-cys by size**
Both glu and its dipeptide glu-cys contain the acidic $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ side chain which is deprotonated to $\text{CO}_2^-$, giving them net negative charge so both move to (+). The free amino acid glu is smaller with lower $M_r$ than the dipeptide glu-cys. For a similar charge, the larger ion moves more slowly through the buffer and support, so the furthest spot E is glu and the intermediate spot F is glu-cys.

Final answer: Spot E: glu (glutamic acid)
Spot F: glu-cys dipeptide
Spot G: cys (cysteine)
Cys remains at the origin because it exists mainly as a zwitterion / is almost neutral, so has no net charge to move in the field.
Glu-cys moves a shorter distance than glu toward the (+) electrode because glu-cys has a greater $M_r$ than glu, so lower charge to mass ratio and lower mobility.
